attempts.raw_response: German-owned businesses faced boycotts and vandalism, while teachers with German names lost their positions and pastors preaching in German were run out of their pulpits. In some towns, citizens who had lived peacefully for decades found themselves accused of sabotage simply because of their heritage. The federal government encouraged this suspicion through the Committee on Public Information, which distributed pamphlets warning of a "German plots" conspiracy. State legislatures passed laws banning the teaching of German and in some cases even forbidding the use of the German language in public. The Espionage Act of 1917 and the Sedition Act of 1918 made it a crime to speak disloyally about the war effort, and over two thousand people were prosecuted under these laws, many of them German-Americans whose only offense was expressing pride in their cultural background.

pair.human_continuation:
A Lutheran minister from a Collinsville-area church was forced to leave the community because he reportedly would not renounce his German citizenship. Throughout the nation, harassment of German immigrants and those of German descent peaked during early 1918.

Lynching of Robert Paul Prager
Prager's application to join UMW Local 1802 was rejected on April 3, 1918. After the union meeting that evening, miners paraded Prager near saloons in Maryville, then warned him to leave that town. Prager was angered to have been rejected by Local 1802 and losing his job. The next morning, he wrote a letter to the Maryville miners, complaining that he had been treated unfairly by Local 1802 President James Fornero. "I have been a union man all times and never once a scab [strikebreaker]," Prager said.
pair.prefix:
Examples of anti-German sentiment were street names being changed and German-language classes dropped in many communities. Groups ranging from the All-Allied Anti-German League to the Boy Spies of America reported any activity they thought suspicious.

In the coal fields of southern Illinois, miners administered extralegal justice against real and perceived enemies: in a kind of charivari, they tarred and feathered some men, and drove others out of town through mob harassment.
